Reducer Behaviors

Reducer Behaviors allow engineers to derive the next immutable state snapshot during pipeline processing. Reducers operate on the current state value and deterministically produce the next state that will be emitted, persisted, and observed.

Reducer Contract Summary

  • Reducers must be pure and side-effect free
  • Reducers must not mutate the incoming state
  • Reducers must return a state value of the same structural shape and type
  • Reducers execute in initialization order
  • Errors during reducer execution propagate as Vault errors

The Reducer contract guarantees that reducer execution is atomic and isolated. If a reducer function throws an error, that error is promoted to a Vault error and immediately terminates the current pipeline execution. The in-flight candidate value is discarded, no state is committed, and no snapshot is emitted. This ensures that reducer failures never result in partially applied state or inconsistent pipeline outcomes. For details on how referential isolation is enforced at every stage boundary, see Pipeline Isolation.

Reducers are the only pipeline stage permitted to change state. They never mutate existing snapshots, never influence pipeline scheduling or control flow, and never emit snapshots directly. Their sole responsibility is to derive the next immutable state value.

Reducer Stage

The Reducer Stage runs after operators and filters and before AfterTap and output layers. Reducers receive the current immutable state snapshot and apply deterministic transformation logic to produce the next state.

A reducer must:

  • Return the current state unchanged
  • Return a new derived state with the same structural shape

Reducers must be pure. They may not mutate the incoming state, and they may not change its structural type. Arrays must remain arrays, objects must remain objects, and primitives must retain their original primitive type. Structural violations result in controlled Vault errors to protect pipeline integrity.

Core Pipeline Stage

The Reducer stage is a core pipeline stage and is always present as part of the FeatureCell lifecycle. However, individual reducer functions are not registered as part of the FeatureCell’s declarative configuration. Instead, reducer functions are attached exclusively through the fluent .reducers() API during FeatureCell initialization, ensuring that state transformation rules are defined explicitly at startup rather than embedded into static cell configuration.

Fluent Reducers() API

A FeatureCell may declare multiple reducers. The fluent .reducers() API accepts an array of reducer functions, which is treated as a declarative, ordered configuration. When provided, reducers are executed in the Processing Layer in the exact order they are listed during initialization.

An empty reducer array is ignored and has no effect on pipeline execution.

Engineer-Supplied Reducer Functions

Reducer functions are supplied by engineers during FeatureCell initialization and execute exclusively within the Reducer stage. Each function is evaluated as a pure, deterministic operation that must preserve the structural contract of the state. Reducers do not own pipeline flow, scheduling, or lifecycle concerns; their sole responsibility is to derive the next immutable state value.

Note

Although multiple reducer functions may be composed, reducer logic should remain narrowly focused and structurally conservative. Overly complex or interdependent reducers can obscure intent and make state evolution difficult to reason about. Reducers are most effective when each function enforces a single, clearly defined transformation.

Reducer Stage Diagram
Available Reducer Behaviors

The Reducer behavior is part of the core pipeline and always present as a stage. Engineers supply reducer functions that are executed by the core reducer behavior during pipeline processing.

Core Reducer Behavior
Behavior Description

withCoreReducerBehavior

input: currentState, reducerFn

Executes an engineer-supplied pure reducer function against the current immutable state snapshot. The reducer must return a new state value or the original state when no change is required.

  • Arrays must return arrays
  • Objects must return objects
  • Primitives must retain their primitive type

Structural mismatches produce controlled Vault errors. This stage is the authoritative mechanism for accumulating, deriving, and finalizing application state.

ReducerFunction<T>
Signature Description
(current: T) => T A pure function that receives the current immutable state snapshot and returns the next state value of the same structural type.
FeatureCell Initialization

The Reducer stage exposes a fluent configuration API that allows engineers to register reducer functions during FeatureCell initialization.

This API does not execute reducers directly. It records an ordered set of reducer functions that are later applied by the Reducer stage during pipeline execution.

Fluent Reducer Configuration
Fluent API Description

.reducers(reducers)

input:

  • reducers: ReducerFunction<T>[]

returns: FeatureCellBaseShape (chainable)

Registers reducer functions for a FeatureCell. Reducers are responsible for producing the next committed state by combining the current state with the resolved pipeline value.

Reducers are executed in the Reduction Layer in the exact order they are registered. This method must be called before initialize(). Multiple calls overwrite prior reducer configuration.

Reducer Function Patterns

The Reducer behavior is a core pipeline construct, but the reducer functions they execute are supplied by engineers. While JavaScript allows many ways to express a function, only a small subset of patterns are safe and appropriate for use in the Reducer stage.

From the pipeline’s perspective, there are only two dimensions that matter:

  • Whether the function depends on instance state
  • Whether the function is deterministic for a given input

The following categories describe the supported and discouraged ways to supply reducer functions, ordered from most to least preferred.

Category A: Pure / Context-Free Functions (Recommended)

Pure reducer functions depend only on their input value and produce a deterministic output. They do not reference this, do not close over mutable external state, and are fully predictable across executions.

This is the safest and most reusable form of reducer function and is recommended whenever possible.

Example 1: Pure Reducer Function

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [
    (current) => ({ ...current, count: current.count + 1 })
  ]
).initialize()
// count is incremented immutably`}}

Example 2: Factory-Generated Pure Reducer Function

{{`export function withFullName() {
  return (emp) => ({
    ...emp,
    fullName: emp.firstName + ' ' + emp.lastName
  });
}

<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [
    withFullName()
  ]
).initialize()`}}

Category B: Instance-Aware but Correctly Bound Reducer Functions (Acceptable)

Reducer functions may reference instance state as long as they are correctly bound to the owning instance. These reducers remain pure with respect to their inputs and are deterministic per FeatureCell instance, but they must not be shared across FeatureCells.

This pattern is acceptable when reducer logic depends on configuration values or state owned by the containing class. Instance-aware reducers must still obey all reducer contracts: immutability, structural preservation, and absence of side effects.

Example 3: Arrow Function Using Instance State

{{`readonly incrementBy = 5;

readonly incrementReducer = (current) => ({
  ...current,
  count: current.count + this.incrementBy
});

<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [this.incrementReducer]
).initialize();

// count is incremented using instance-scoped configuration`}}

Example 4: Bound Instance Method

{{`public normalizeName(current) {
  return {
    ...current,
    name: current.name.trim().toLowerCase()
  };
}

<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [this.normalizeName.bind(this)]
).initialize();

// reducer logic is instance-bound and deterministic per FeatureCell`}}

Category C: Delegating Reducer Functions (Reducers Only)

Reducer functions may delegate their implementation to class methods or helper functions, provided that those methods remain pure and derive their output solely from the reducer’s input value.

Unlike filters or stepwise behaviors, reducers do not participate in pipeline control flow or admission logic. As a result, delegating reducer logic to standalone methods is safe as long as those methods do not depend on external mutable state and do not mutate the incoming value.

This pattern is useful for organizing complex reducer logic, sharing implementation across reducers, or improving testability through method extraction.

Example 5: Delegating Reducer Method

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [
    (employees) => this.partialReducerStandaloneMethod(employees)
  ]
).initialize();

// reducer logic is delegated but remains pure and deterministic`}}

Category D: Inline Lambda Reducers (Allowed, Use Sparingly)

Inline lambda functions are allowed, but they are easier to misuse. Because they are often written inline, it is easy to accidentally close over mutable variables or embed complex logic that is difficult to test or reuse.

Inline reducers are best reserved for trivial, self-contained transformations.

Example 6: Inline Conditional Reducer

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [
    (current) => {
      if (!current.items?.length) return current;
      return { ...current, items: [...current.items].sort() };
    }
  ]
).initialize()`}}
Reducer Function Anti-Patterns

Category E: Mutation or External State (Discouraged)

Reducer functions that mutate state or depend on external mutable variables are unsafe. They violate immutability guarantees and undermine deterministic pipeline behavior.

If a reducer requires state, that state must be instance-scoped and explicitly bound. External mutable variables should never influence reducer behavior.

Example 7: Discouraged Mutation

{{`<employeeCell\|this>.vault.reducers(
  [
    (current) => {
      current.count++; // ❌ mutation
      return current;
    }
  ]
).initialize()

// ❌ Vault error: reducers must not mutate state`}}
Reducer Function Summary

Reducer Function Comparison

The following table summarizes the practical differences between the reducer function styles demonstrated above. While all valid examples may execute correctly, they differ in reusability, testability, and long-term safety.

Reducer Function Characteristics
Dimension Examples 1 / 2
Pure Reducer Functions 		Examples 3 / 4
Instance-Bound Reducers 		Example 5
Delegating Reducer 		Example 6
Inline Lambda Reducer 		Example 7
Mutation / External State
Purity ✅ ⚠️ Instance-scoped ⚠️ Delegated ⚠️ ❌
Determinism ✅ ⚠️ Per instance ⚠️ Per instance ⚠️ ❌
Safety for Pipelines ✅ ✅ ✅ ⚠️ ❌
Reusability High Medium Medium Low None
Testability High Medium High Lower Low
Risk of Accidental Closure Low Low Low Higher High
Intended Lifespan Long-lived Instance-limited Instance-limited Ephemeral Unacceptable
Recommended Usage Preferred Acceptable Acceptable Use sparingly Discouraged

Summary Rule

Any reducer function must be pure with respect to its input and must return a value of the same structural type. Reducers may be instance-aware or delegated, but they must never mutate state or depend on external mutable variables. All reducer behavior must remain deterministic within the owning FeatureCell.

Examples

Reducers are applied by supplying pure reducer functions that operate on the current immutable state value during pipeline execution. The following examples illustrate valid and invalid reducer function behavior.

Example 1: Basic Increment Reducer

{{`@FeatureCell<Employee[][]>('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[][]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault.reducers(
      [
        (current) => ({
          ...current,
          count: current.count + 1
        })
      ]
    ).initialize()
  }
}
// count is incremented immutably`}}

Example 2: Adding Derived Fields

{{`@FeatureCell<Employee[][]>('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[][]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault.reducers(
      [
        (emp) => ({
          ...emp,
          fullName: emp.firstName + ' ' + emp.lastName,
          senior: emp.years > 10
        })
      ]
    ).initialize()
  }
}
// derived fields are added immutably`}}

Example 3: Conditional Reducer

{{`@FeatureCell<Employee[][]>('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[][]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault.reducers(
      [
        (current) => {
          if (!current.items?.length) return current;
          return {
            ...current,
            items: [...current.items].sort()
          };
        }
      ]
    ).initialize()
  }
}
// state changes only when items exist`}}

Example 4: Returning the Same Value (No Change)

{{`@FeatureCell<Employee[][]>('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[][]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault.reducers(
      [
        (current) => current
      ]
    ).initialize()
  }
}
// no state change — safe and legal`}}

Reducer Anti-Pattern Examples

The following examples demonstrate invalid reducer function behavior. These patterns violate the Reducer contract by mutating the current state value or by returning a value that does not preserve the original structural type. Such violations are detected and rejected by the Vault to protect pipeline integrity and ensure deterministic state evolution. 

{{`@FeatureCell<Employee[][]>('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[][]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault.reducers(
      [
        (current) => {
          current.count++; // ❌ mutation
          return current;
        }
      ]
    ).initialize()
  }
}

// ❌ Vault error: reducers must not mutate state`}}

Example 6: Invalid — Returning Wrong Shape

{{`@FeatureCell<Employee[][]>('employees')
@Injectable({
  providedIn: 'root'
})
export class EmployeeService {
  private readonly vault = injectVault<Employee[][]>(EmployeeService);

  constructor() {
    // Apply one or more reducers during initialization
    this.vault.reducers(
      [
        (current) => 123 // ❌ incorrect type
      ]
    ).initialize()
  }
}

// ❌ Vault error: reducer returned incompatible state type`}}

Example 5: Invalid — Mutating the Input

{{`employeeCell.reducers(
  [
    (current) => {
      current.count++; // ❌ mutation
      return current;
    }
  ]
).initialize()

// ❌ Vault error: reducers must not mutate state`}}

Example 6: Invalid — Returning Wrong Shape

{{`employeeCell.reducers(
  [
    (current) => 123 // ❌ incorrect type
  ]
).initialize()

// ❌ Vault error: reducer returned incompatible state type`}}
